entry: Practice of managing information from an organization to the public in order to influence perception. Public relations (PR) differs from publicity in that PR is controlled internally, whereas publicity is contributed by external parties. PR seeks media exposure, often without direct payment, known as earned media, which distinguishes it from paid [[Advertising|advertising]]. PR and [[Journalism|journalism]] share close media relations, but journalism reports events with objectivity, while PR presents developments in ways that support the interests of the organization it represents. Practitioners write press releases, arrange interviews for spokespeople, manage [[Company|company]] reputation and crises, and produce content for [[Social media|social media]] and [[Website|websites]]. The aim is to inform the public, customers, investors and employees, and to persuade them to maintain a favorable view of the organization.

Transport made available for use by the general public, typically operating on fixed routes and schedules for a standardized fare. Common modes include city buses, trams, rapid transit, passenger trains and ferries. Intercity service is provided mainly by coaches, intercity [[Train|rail]] and [[Airline|airlines]], with [[High-speed rail]] networks under development in several regions. Systems vary widely by region. In [[Japan]], many urban networks are run by private companies, often integrated with real estate development. In North America, mass transit is usually operated by municipal or regional transit authorities funded by fares, local taxes and government subsidies. The earliest public transport was water transport: ferries appear in [[Greek mythology]], and in ancient Egypt canals carried freight around the [[Aswan]] cataract.

Capital and largest city of Puebla state, Mexico. Founded in 1531 as a planned Spanish city between the indigenous settlements of Tlaxcala and Cholula, it lies on the main route between [[Mexico City]] and the Atlantic port of [[Veracruz (city)|Veracruz]]. It is the fourth-largest city in Mexico, after Mexico City, [[Monterrey]] and [[Guadalajara]], with a current population of 3,344,000. Its history and architecture, ranging from Renaissance to Mexican Baroque, led to its designation as a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1987. The city is known for mole poblano, chiles en nogada and Talavera pottery, but its economy is mostly industrial. It has the world's largest Volkswagen factory outside Germany, and many suppliers to Volkswagen and Audi plants have opened factories in the metropolitan area.

Japanese [[Anime|anime]] television series and its franchise. Created by Magica Quartet and animated by Shaft, it follows middle school girls who make contracts to become magical girls and fight creatures called witches. The first 10 episodes aired between January and March 2011. The franchise includes a [[Manga|manga]] adaptation, a [[PlayStation Portable]] game and several films, and the series received widespread critical acclaim for its complex narrative and unconventional approach to the magical girl subgenre. Each [[Blu-ray]] volume sold more than 50,000 copies in Japan.

Caribbean archipelago and unincorporated territory of the [[United States]], officially the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico. Located about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) southeast of [[Miami]], it has approximately 3.2 million people and 78 municipalities. Spanish and English are official languages, though Spanish predominates. The island was settled by Indigenous peoples, including the [[Taíno]]. Spain claimed it after [[Christopher Columbus]] arrived in 1493, and it remained Spanish until the [[Spanish–American War]] of 1898, after which the United States acquired it. Puerto Ricans have been U.S. citizens since 1917, but residents are disenfranchised from federal elections, and the territory sends a nonvoting representative to Congress. Its political status remains a subject of debate. Manufacturing, mainly of pharmaceuticals, petrochemicals and electronics, and tourism are the major sectors of the economy.

Genus of three species of small pelagic [[Seabird|seabirds]] in the [[Auk|auk]] family, *Fratercula*. Puffins feed mainly by diving and breed in large colonies on coastal cliffs or offshore islands. The Atlantic puffin lives in the North Atlantic, while the tufted and horned puffins are found in the [[Pacific Ocean|North Pacific]]. All species have predominantly black or black-and-white plumage and large beaks that are brightly colored during the breeding season, when the colorful outer part of the bill is shed afterward. The name was originally applied to the fatty, salted meat of young Manx shearwaters.

Series of annual American awards for achievements in journalism, arts and letters. Administered by [[Columbia University]] in [[New York City]], the prizes were funded by the will of [[Joseph Pulitzer]], a Hungarian-American newspaper publisher, and the first were awarded in June 1917. Of the 23 awards, 15 are for journalism and eight for books, drama and music. Three finalists are named for each award, and winners are chosen each spring after recommendations from the Pulitzer Prize Board. Each award carries a certificate and a $15,000 prize, except Public Service, where the winning news organization receives a gold medal.

Wheel on an axle or shaft that guides a taut [[Rope|rope]], [[Chain|chain]] or belt, changing its direction or transferring power. A grooved pulley wheel is also called a sheave. The earliest evidence comes from [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] in the Twelfth Dynasty (1991–1802 BC) and from [[Mesopotamia]] in the early 2nd millennium BC. [[Hero of Alexandria]] identified the pulley as one of six simple machines used to lift weights. A block and tackle, which combines pulleys, gives a mechanical advantage equal to the number of rope sections supporting the moving block. Plutarch recounts that [[Archimedes]] used compound pulleys to draw a fully laden ship toward him as if it were gliding through water. Pulleys also drive belts and chains that transmit power between shafts.

Medical specialty concerned with diseases of the respiratory tract, also called pneumology, respirology or respiratory medicine. Pulmonology is a branch of [[Medicine|internal medicine]] closely related to intensive care, since pulmonologists often manage patients who need mechanical ventilation. They treat conditions such as [[Pneumonia]], [[Asthma]], [[Tuberculosis]], [[Emphysema]] and complicated chest infections, and work closely with [[Cardiology]] and cardiothoracic surgery departments. Diagnosis considers hereditary diseases such as cystic fibrosis and exposure to toxicants such as tobacco smoke and [[Asbestos]]. [[Galen]] had theorized that blood crossed the heart through pores in the septum; in the 13th century, Ibn al-Nafis argued that blood instead passes through the lungs, believed by many to be the first scientific description of pulmonary circulation.

1994 American crime film written and directed by [[Quentin Tarantino]] from a story he conceived with Roger Avary. Its four intertwining tales of crime and violence in [[Los Angeles]] unfold out of chronological order. The cast includes [[John Travolta]], [[Samuel L. Jackson]], [[Bruce Willis]] and [[Uma Thurman]]. The film won the Palme d'Or at the 1994 Cannes Film Festival and received seven nominations at the 67th [[Academy Awards]], winning Best Original Screenplay. Its success revived Travolta's career. Critics regard it as Tarantino's magnum opus and a touchstone of postmodern film. In 2013 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

Rotating [[Neutron star|neutron star]] that emits beams of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] from its magnetic poles. The beams are observable only when they point toward Earth, much as a [[Lighthouse|lighthouse]] is visible only when its light faces an observer. Pulses recur at highly regular intervals, ranging from milliseconds to seconds. In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, working with Antony Hewish, detected the first pulsar in data from a [[Radio telescope|radio telescope]] she helped build; the signals were at first nicknamed LGM-1, for little green men. In 1983 some pulsars were found to keep time more accurately than [[Atomic clock|atomic clocks]]. Observations of a pulsar in a binary neutron star system indirectly confirmed the existence of [[Gravitational wave|gravitational radiation]]. The first [[Exoplanet|extrasolar planets]] were discovered around a pulsar in 1992.

Rhythmic expansion and contraction of an [[Artery|artery]] in response to the heartbeat, which can be felt at sites such as the neck, wrist, groin and behind the knee. It is most commonly measured at the wrist or neck in adults and at the brachial artery in infants, and is recorded in beats per minute. [[Galen]] may have been the first physiologist to describe the pulse, which gives a trained observer a tactile estimate of systolic blood pressure. In healthy people the pulse rate is close to the [[Heart|heart]] rate, but in a pulse deficit some heartbeats do not produce a pulse at the periphery. A regular pulse is normal, whereas an irregular one may result from [[Atrial fibrillation|atrial fibrillation]]. A weak pulse may indicate low cardiac output, as in [[Shock (circulatory)|shock]]. Pulse oximeters estimate oxygen saturation by measuring light absorbed by [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]].

Typically light-colored volcanic rock made of extremely vesicular volcanic glass; its powdered form is called pumicite. Pumice forms when gas-rich [[Magma|magma]] is ejected from a [[Volcano|volcano]], where rapid depressurization and cooling freeze gas bubbles into the glass. Its porosity of 64–85% by volume lets it float on water, possibly for years. Floating pumice can form rafts that are hazardous to ships. Unlike dark, denser scoria, pumice is used as an [[Abrasive|abrasive]] and as a lightweight aggregate in [[Concrete|concrete]]. Major deposits occur in [[Oregon]], [[New Mexico]] and [[California]].

Public utility building containing pumps and equipment for moving fluids from one place to another. Pumping stations are critical to [[Water supply|water supply]], the drainage of low-lying land, [[Canal|canal]] systems and the removal of sewage. Canals lose water through [[Lock (water navigation)|lock]] use and leakage, and a pumping station can supply the water where no other source exists. Draining land below [[Sea level]] requires pumping water upward into channels that drain to the sea, a method pioneered in the [[Victorian era]] in The Fens of the U.K. Wastewater stations handle sewage, and submersible designs are more compact and less visible. Pumped-storage hydroelectric schemes use pumping stations to move water between reservoirs at different elevations, storing and generating energy.

Cultivated winter squash in the genus [[Cucurbita]], most often applied to round, orange-colored varieties. Its fruit is a [[Berry (botany)|berry]] called a pepo, with a thick shell enclosing edible seeds and pulp. Some pumpkins, such as *C. pepo*, are among the oldest known domesticated plants, cultivated between 7000 BCE and 5500 BCE in [[Mesoamerica]]. Many North American Indigenous societies grew them with [[Maize|maize]] and [[Bean|beans]] in the Three Sisters system. Giant pumpkins, mostly *C. maxima*, can exceed a [[Tonne|tonne]]; the heaviest recorded pumpkin weighed 1,246.9 kg in October 2023. Pumpkin pie is a traditional Thanksgiving dish in Canada and the [[United States]], and pumpkins are carved as jack-o'-lanterns for [[Halloween]].

Mountain on the island of [[New Guinea]], the highest peak of an island on Earth and the highest in [[Indonesia]] and [[Oceania]]. It rises 4,884 m (16,024 ft) in the Sudirman Range of Central Papua. The peak is also called Carstensz Pyramid, after the Dutch explorer Jan Carstenszoon, who was the first European to sight its glaciers, in 1623. Puncak Jaya is often counted among the Seven Summits and is the highest point of the Central Range, a chain formed in the late [[Miocene]] by an oblique collision between the Australian and Pacific plates. Its summit is free of ice, but its glaciers have retreated significantly since the 1850s. The nearby Grasberg gold and copper mine, the world's second-largest gold mine, lies about 4 km west of the peak.

Stiff paper card that stores digital information through the presence or absence of holes in predefined positions. Developed over the 19th and 20th centuries, punched cards were first used to control [[Loom|looms]] and later to record census data. Basile Bouchon controlled a loom with punched holes in paper tape in 1725, and Joseph Marie Jacquard linked punched cards into chains in 1804. [[Charles Babbage]] described number cards for his Calculating Engine, but there is no evidence that he built a practical example. Herman Hollerith developed punched-card data processing for the 1890 U.S. census. The IBM 12-row, 80-column format came to dominate the industry, and many early [[Computer|computers]] used punched cards for programs and data. Magnetic tape later replaced them, but the 80-column standard persists in some command-line interfaces.

City in [[Maharashtra]], western India, on the [[Deccan Plateau]], and administrative headquarters of Pune district. It is the largest city in Maharashtra by area, though second to [[Mumbai]] by population. The Pune Metropolitan Region had 7.2 million residents in the 2011 census, making it the seventh-most populous metropolitan area in India. Pune is one of India's largest information technology hubs and a major automobile and manufacturing center, and it is often called the Oxford of the East for its educational institutions. In the 18th century the city was the seat of the Peshwas, the prime ministers of the [[Maratha Empire]]. It was seized by the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] during the Third Anglo-Maratha War and later became a center of resistance to the [[British Raj]]. The city was known as Poona until 1978.

Three wars fought between the [[Roman Republic]] and the [[Carthage|Carthaginian]] Empire from 264 to 146 BC, beginning with a conflict over [[Sicily]]. The First Punic War ended in 241 BC with Carthage defeated, and Sicily became the first Roman province. In the Second Punic War, which began in 218 BC, the Carthaginian general [[Hannibal]] crossed the Alps and campaigned in Italy for 14 years before being defeated at Zama in 202 BC. Rome declared the Third Punic War in 149 BC. In 146 BC the Romans stormed the city, sacked it and demolished it, and its territory became the Roman province of Africa. The ruins lie east of modern [[Tunis]] on the North African coast.

Imposition of an undesirable or unpleasant outcome on an individual or group in response to breaking a norm or rule. The term is used in [[Criminal law|criminal justice]] and elsewhere, as in [[Child|child]] discipline. Philosophers have justified punishment as a means of deterring wrongdoing, rehabilitating offenders, incapacitating the dangerous or giving justice to those who deserve it. Penalties range from reprimands, removal of privileges and fines to [[Prison|imprisonment]], [[Amputation|amputation]] and the death penalty. [[Aristotle]] wrote extensively on the ethics of imposing pain. In psychology, following B.F. Skinner, punishment reduces a behavior through an unpleasant stimulus or the removal of a pleasant one, and is identified only when the behavior decreases. Punishment can also be part of [[Pedagogy|pedagogy]], alongside rewards.

Geographical, ethnolinguistic and historical region of [[South Asia]] in the northwest, comprising parts of [[Pakistan]] and northwestern [[India]]. The name combines the Persian words for five and water, meaning Land of Five Waters, a reference to the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej and Beas rivers, tributaries of the [[Indus River]]. Settlements developed along these rivers as early as the Indus Valley civilization, around 3000 BCE. Agriculture has been central to Punjabi culture, and after the [[Green Revolution]] of the mid-1960s to mid-1970s the region became known as the breadbasket of both India and Pakistan. Partition in 1947 divided the region along religious lines, and Punjabi Muslims form the majority in the Pakistani part, while Punjabi Sikhs are the majority in the Indian part. [[Lahore]] is its largest city and historic capital.

State in northwestern [[India]], sharing an international border with Pakistan's Punjab province to the west. [[Chandigarh]] is its capital and is shared with [[Haryana]]. The state covers 50,362 sq km and has over 27 million inhabitants. Sikhs (57.7%) and Hindus (38.5%) form the dominant religious groups, and Punjabi, written in the Gurmukhi script, is the official language. The region was annexed by the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] in 1849 and partitioned in 1947. In 1966 the state was reorganized along linguistic lines into its present form. A separatist insurgency occurred in the 1980s, and the society remains predominantly agrarian.

Province of [[Pakistan]] with over 127 million people, the most populous in the country and the second most populous subnational polity in the world. Its capital and largest city is [[Lahore]]; other major cities include [[Faisalabad]], [[Rawalpindi]], [[Gujranwala]] and [[Multan]]. Located in the central-eastern part of the country, it has Pakistan's largest economy and is considered the breadbasket of the nation. Punjab is also the most industrialized province, and about 40 percent of its population is urban. Punjabi Muslims form the majority, and their culture has been strongly influenced by Islam and [[Sufism]], with many Sufi shrines across the province. Several sites in the province are [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]], including the Lahore Fort, the Shalimar Gardens and the excavations at Taxila.

Indo-Aryan language of the Indo-Iranian branch of the [[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]] family, spoken mainly by the Punjabi people of the Punjab region of Pakistan and India. It has more than 156 million speakers across its varieties, and in Pakistan it is the most widely spoken native language, with 123.2 million speakers according to the 2023 census. Punjabi is written in two standard scripts: Shahmukhi, based on the Perso-Arabic script, in Pakistan, and Gurmukhi, based on Indic scripts, in India. Its vocabulary derives largely from [[Sanskrit]] through Prakrit, while its high-register speech draws heavily on [[Arabic]] and Persian. It is a tonal language, which is unusual among Indo-Aryan languages. Standard Punjabi is based on the Majhi dialect, and the language is official in the Indian state of Punjab. Significant diaspora communities speak it in [[Canada]], the [[United Kingdom]] and the [[United States]].

Genre of [[Rock music|rock music]] that emerged in the mid-1970s, rooted in 1950s [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]] and 1960s garage rock. Punk bands rejected the overproduction and corporate nature of mainstream arena rock, typically producing short, fast-paced songs with rough vocals and anti-establishment themes. Many artists embraced a do-it-yourself ethic, self-producing their recordings and releasing them through independent labels. Early scenes centered on the [[Ramones]] and [[Patti Smith]] in New York City and on the [[Sex Pistols]] and [[The Clash|the Clash]] in England. By 1977 punk had spread worldwide, giving rise to post-punk, new wave and hardcore. After [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]] broke into the mainstream in the 1990s through bands such as [[Nirvana (band)|Nirvana]], punk saw renewed major-label interest.
